Here's how **looting** works in Frosthaven:

---

## The Loot Ability

> "*Loot X* is an ability that allows a figure to loot all loot tokens and treasure tiles within range X, including any in their current hex. This ability is unaffected by the presence of figures or overlay tiles. If there are no loot tokens or treasure tiles within the specified range, the ability cannot be performed."

*(Rulebook, passage 111)*

---

## Looting Tokens

When a **loot token** is looted, it is removed from the map. Then:

- **Monsters:** Nothing else happens — they remove the token but gain nothing.
- **Characters:** Draw one card from the **loot deck** (unless it's empty).

---

## Loot Card Types

Each scenario has a custom loot deck built from these four card types:

- 💰 **Money** — 1–3 coins, converted to gold based on scenario level (gained at end of scenario).
- 🪵 **Material Resources** (lumber, metal, hide) — varying amounts based on number of characters (gained at end of scenario).
- 🌿 **Herb Resources** (arrowvine, axenut, corpsecap, flamefruit, rockroot, snowthistle) — one herb each (gained at end of scenario).
- 🎲 **Random Item** — Immediately draw from the random item deck and add it to your item pool. You may use it for the rest of the scenario even if it exceeds your item limit.

> "Money and resources looted during a scenario are not gained until the end of the scenario, but random items are gained immediately when looted."

*(Rulebook, passage 67)*

---

## Looting Treasure Tiles

When a **treasure tile** is looted, it is removed from the map. **Monsters cannot loot treasure tiles.** If it's a numbered treasure, look it up in the Treasure Index and apply the effect — only the looting character gains the reward (unless it's a random item blueprint or random scenario).

Here's how the recommended scenario level is calculated in Frosthaven:

## Recommended Scenario Level

> At recommended difficulty, the scenario level is equal to the average level of the characters divided by 2 (rounded up).

**Example:** If all characters are level 2, the average (2) ÷ 2 = 1, so the scenario is still level 1. A character would need to reach level 3 before the scenario level potentially increases.

---

### Scenario Level Table

| Scenario Level | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Monster Level | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
| Gold Conversion | 2 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| Trap Damage | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 |
| Hazardous Terrain | 1 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 4 |
| Bonus Experience | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 | 12 | 14 | 16 | 18 |

---

### Adjustments

- **You can set any level from 0–7** at the start of a scenario — decrease it if your party is struggling, increase it to stay challenged.
- **Solo mode (or Open Information variant):** Add 1 to the average character level *before* dividing by 2 and rounding up, to account for reduced uncertainty. For example, three level 4 characters normally gives scenario level 2, but in solo mode it becomes level 3.

*(Rulebook, passages 67–68 and 203)*

Here's how *advantage* works with attack modifier cards in Frosthaven, based on the rulebook:

---

## Advantage — Drawing Two Modifiers

When an attack has *advantage*, the attacker **draws two modifier cards** and gets to use one of them:
- A **monster** always uses the **better** one.
- A **character** may use **either** one (their choice).

---

## Rolling Modifiers with Advantage

The interaction with *rolling modifiers* adds some complexity:

1. If the **first draw** is a rolling modifier, keep drawing one at a time until you hit a **non-rolling modifier**.
2. Then draw **one more** modifier, ignoring any rolling icon on it.
3. You now compare the **first non-rolling modifier** and the **final modifier**:
   - **All initial rolling modifiers are used** (their bonuses/effects apply).
   - You choose **whichever of the last two modifiers** you prefer.

4. If the **first draw is not a rolling modifier** but the **second draw is**, the rolling icon on the second card is **still ignored** — it does not chain further draws.

---

## Ambiguity

When it's unclear which modifier is "better" (e.g., one card adds an elemental infusion or a condition instead of a numeric bonus), **any non-numeric effect is treated as having a positive but undefined value**. If there's still ambiguity, you must use the **card drawn first**.

---

## Advantage + Disadvantage Cancel Out

> "An attack cannot gain multiple instances of advantage or disadvantage. If an attack has both advantage and disadvantage, it is considered to have neither."

---

## Ranged Attacks vs. Adjacent Enemies

Any **ranged attack targeting an adjacent enemy** automatically gains *disadvantage*, which would cancel out any *advantage* the attacker might have.

*(Rulebook, passages 96–97)*

*(Rulebook, passage 125)*

**When to declare:** During the **Card Selection** step, a character may declare a long rest instead of selecting two cards to play. This constitutes their **entire turn** for the round and is performed on **initiative 99**.

---

## *Loot* Ability

> **"Loot X"** is an ability that allows a figure to loot all money tokens and treasure tiles within range X, including any in their current hex. This ability is unaffected by the presence of figures or overlay tiles. If there are no money tokens or treasure tiles within the specified range, the ability cannot be performed.

*(Rulebook, passage 132)*

---

## End-of-Turn Looting

> Characters must loot any money tokens or treasure tiles present in their hex **at the end of their turn**. No figures beside characters perform end-of-turn looting.

*(Rulebook, passage 156)*

This means characters automatically loot their own hex at the end of every turn — no *Loot* ability needed for that. Monsters and summons do **not** perform end-of-turn looting.

---

## What Happens When You Loot

**Money tokens:**
- Removed from the map when looted.
- If a **monster** loots a money token (via a *Loot* ability on its card), the token is simply removed — nothing else happens.
- If a **character** loots a money token, they place it on their character mat.

**Treasure tiles:**
- Removed from the map when looted.
- **Monsters cannot loot treasure tiles.**
- If it is a numbered treasure, reference the Treasure Index and apply the effect (only the looting character gains the reward, unless it is a random item design or random scenario).
- If the looting character gains a duplicate item they already own, they must give it to another character or sell it immediately.

*(Rulebook, passage 133)*

---

## Monster *Loot* Abilities

Some monsters have *Loot* abilities on their ability cards. In those cases:
- The monster loots all money tokens within the specified range, removing them from the map.
- Those money tokens are **not** dropped again when the monster dies.
- Monsters are **still unable** to loot treasure tiles.

*(Rulebook, passage 182)*

Here's how the recommended scenario level is calculated in **Gloomhaven (2nd Edition)**:

> At recommended difficulty, the scenario level is equal to the average level of the characters **divided by 2** (rounded up).

**Formula:** `Average Character Level ÷ 2 (rounded up)`

**Example:** If all characters are level 2, the average (2) ÷ 2 = 1, so the scenario is still level 1. Only once a character reaches level 3 would the scenario level potentially increase to 2.

---

### Adjustments

- **You can override it:** At the start of any scenario, the level can be set freely from **0–7**. Lower it if your party is struggling; raise it for a greater challenge.
- **Solo mode** (one player controlling two or more characters): Add 1 to the average character level *before* dividing by 2 and rounding up, to compensate for the coordination advantage. Formula: `(Average Character Level + 1) ÷ 2 (rounded up)`
- **Open Information variant:** Use the same adjusted formula as solo mode.

Here's how *Advantage* and *Disadvantage* work with attack modifier cards in **Gloomhaven (2nd Edition)**:

---

## Advantage

> With **advantage**, the attacker draws two modifiers and uses one of them. A monster always uses the better one, but a character may use either one.

## Disadvantage

> With **disadvantage**, the attacker draws two modifiers and always uses the worse one.

---

## Rolling Modifiers with Advantage/Disadvantage

When rolling modifiers are involved, things get more complex:

> If the first draw with advantage or disadvantage is a rolling modifier, the attacker draws additional modifiers, one at a time, until a non-rolling modifier is drawn. **They then draw one more modifier and ignore any rolling icon on it.**

Then, the comparison is made between the last two drawn cards:

- **With *Advantage*:** The attacker uses all the initial rolling modifiers **plus** whichever of the final two non-rolling modifiers they choose.
- **With *Disadvantage*:** The attacker **ignores** all the initial rolling modifiers and uses whichever of the final two modifiers is **worse**.

---

## Example (from the rulebook)

An attack has *Advantage* and the first modifier drawn has a rolling icon — so a second modifier is drawn, but it also has a rolling icon, so a third (final) modifier is drawn. The initial rolling modifier and the better of the last two are used.

---

**(Source: Gloomhaven 2nd Edition Rulebook, passage 103)**

**Core Definition**

> **Poison:** All attacks targeting the figure gain "+1 [Attack Modifier star icon]." Poison is removed when the figure is healed but, unlike wound, poison prevents the heal from increasing the figure's current hit point value.

So in practice:
- Any attack made against a *Poisoned* figure gets **+1 to the attack modifier draw** (the attacker draws one extra modifier card and uses the better result — i.e., *Advantage*-like bonus on the modifier deck).

> **Note:** A single heal can remove both *Wound* and *Poison* from a figure. However, if *Poison* is present, the hit point increase from that heal is prevented.

*Poison* is removed by healing, but the heal does **no HP recovery** — it only clears the condition.

---

**Additional FAQ Clarifications** *(Official FAQ, last updated 2026-04-19)*

- *Poison* is **not stackable** — if multiple sources try to apply *Poison* to the same target in the same attack, only one instance is applied.
- Objectives **cannot** gain *Poison* or any other condition.
- If a figure is immune to *Poison* (e.g., a Living Corpse scenario ally), you can still attempt to give it *Poison* — it just won't take effect.
- A figure with *Safeguard* that would receive *Poison* — only one instance is blocked (relevant since *Poison* doesn't stack, this effectively means Safeguard prevents it entirely).
